front.title: Continuity Evaluation of Agent Delegation Records

abstract.t: The AUDIT architecture defines records that capture the user's intent, delegation, authorization state, and the actions that agents take across trust boundaries. Records alone don't answer the question an auditor, an operator, or a relying party asks next: did what was executed stay within the authority the user delegated?

This document defines a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over such records. The outcomes are preserved, violated, and unresolved. A violated outcome names the invariant that was broken and the party whose own signed record departed from authority first. An unresolved outcome names the evidence that is missing; missing evidence is never treated as success. The document also defines the claim model the evaluation needs, the roles permitted to sign each record, a signed statement of what a call did or did not execute, a portable verdict record, a mapping onto the AUDIT record types, and interoperable test vectors. It is derived from the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP).

section.name: Introduction
section.t: AI agents act through chains of delegation: a user to an agent, an agent to sub-agents, and agents to tools, adapters, and services. Each hop can widen what is done relative to what was asked. Common examples:

list.t: an approval for one command is reused for another;
a sub-agent receives broader scope than its parent held;
untrusted content steers a mutation;
an adapter maps a tool call to an effect that differs from the one declared;
a gateway refusal is later read as an executed action, or a lost response is read as a failure;
a decision made after the fact, from an audit log, is presented as if it had prevented the action.

section.t: defines Interaction, Action, Delegation, and Authorization Transition records, and the propagation of audit context, so that these chains can be reconstructed. Its Auditor role determines whether recorded behaviour matched the authorization in force at the time.
This document specifies that determination. Given a set of records, it specifies:

list.t: a claim model that makes delegated authority machine-checkable ();
signer roles, so that a record counts as evidence only when it is signed by a party entitled to make it ();
call statements, so that "nothing was executed" and "the outcome is unknown" are distinguishable from each other and from an executed action ();
invariants that a chain of records must satisfy (I1 to I11);
a deterministic evaluation procedure that returns preserved, violated, or unresolved, with the deciding invariant, the party at fault, and the missing evidence ();
a portable, signed verdict record, so that a second auditor can check a first auditor's conclusion ();
test vectors, so that independent verifiers can demonstrate that they agree.

section.t: The evaluation can run before an effect, when an enforcement point decides on the predicted effect, or after the fact, when an auditor evaluates recorded effects. It never treats missing evidence as success, and it never treats a post-execution decision as a block.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: This document uses the roles of : User, Agent, Tool/Service, Auditing Service, Audit Store, Transparency Log, and Auditor. It adds:

dd.t: a signed claim set issued for a principal, stating what an agent may do on the principal's behalf.
an optional claim set derived from a single request (for example, a prompt), narrower than the mandate.
a declared call to a tool or service, made under a mandate (possibly delegated).
what was actually executed at the boundary where the action took effect.
the party that produced the effect record or call statement.
the observer's signed account of one call: what it executed, or that it executed nothing, and how many effect records belong to the call.
the set of records a verifier evaluates together.
an entity that runs the evaluation in .

section.name: Relationship to the AUDIT Architecture

texttable.c: binding to the exact effect or effects, I8
I7, I11, binding to the exact invocation
liveness at the invocation and at each effect, I6

section.t: Mandates and delegations commonly originate in OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange chains . Records MAY be carried as COSE_Sign1 objects , and MAY be registered with a transparency service , which makes selective omission of records detectable. Conversation records such as can supply the Interaction Records from which mandates, intents and approvals are taken.

This document doesn't define new transport or storage. It requires only that records carry the fields listed in , and that records can be linked using the AUDIT audit context: trace, parent, actor, and on-behalf-of.

section.name: Related Work
section.t: Most related work grants or checks authority before an agent acts. This document evaluates whether what was executed stayed within that authority, and the two are complementary.

list.t: The Delegation Receipt Protocol has the user sign an authorization object that is checked before execution. Such an object can serve as the mandate whose claims this document evaluates.

Authenticated delegation for AI agents proposes scoped, verifiable delegation credentials that extend OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0. Those credentials are another source of mandates and delegations. GNAP negotiates delegated authorization across multiple parties; its grants can likewise be recorded as mandates.

Work on infrastructure for AI agents identifies attribution and incident response as functions that require shared infrastructure outside the agent. The evaluation in supplies one verifiable input to both.

The DIF threat model for delegated authority argues that delegated authority commonly fails at the moment of action rather than at issuance, and asks for execution-time evaluation. compares existing authorization specifications against a set of criteria. This document addresses the execution-time and after-the-fact evaluation those documents call for, and does not define a new credential format.

The NCCoE concept paper on agent identity and authorization covers identification, authorization, auditing, and non-repudiation for agents using existing standards. The records and outcomes defined here are one way to make the auditing and non-repudiation goals checkable.

Prompt-injection benchmarks and defenses, such as AgentDojo and CaMeL , detect or prevent untrusted content from steering an agent. When such steering produces an effect outside the user's mandate, this document reports it as violated (I2 or I4), independent of how the injection was detected.

section.name: Claim Model
section.t: A claim set is C = (G, A⁻, R⁻, D, E, V, P, K, B, L), where:

list.t: G is the set of grants. Each grant is a pair (A, R) of canonical action and resource patterns, and permits its actions on its resources. A claim set with plain action and resource lists has one grant. A list of grants expresses permissions such as "read the documents, write the reports" that a single product of actions and resources cannot express without also permitting "write the documents";
A⁻ and R⁻ are sets of action and resource patterns that are denied even when a grant would permit them;
D is a set of (data class, recipient class) pairs;
E is the effect ceiling, an element of the totally ordered set read < write_local < write_shared < external_send < destructive < financial;
V is the validity interval;
P is the purpose;
K is the delegation budget (remaining depth);
B is an OPTIONAL risk budget in points;
L is an OPTIONAL list of limits on quantities ().

section.t: C1 ⊑ C2 (C1 is equal to or narrower than C2) holds if and only if: every grant of C1 lies within a single grant of C2 (its actions subsumed by that grant's actions and its resources by that grant's resources); every pattern in A2⁻ and R2⁻ is subsumed by some pattern in A1⁻ or R1⁻ respectively (denies only grow); D1 ⊆ D2; E1 ≤ E2; V1 ⊆ V2; P1 = P2 or P2 is unrestricted; the depth rule holds (if K2 is present, K2 > 0 and K1 < K2); B1 ≤ B2 when B2 is present; and no limit of C1 is higher than a limit of C2 in the same unit, actions and period. A child MAY add limits.
The meet C1 ⊓ C2 takes the pairwise intersection of grants and is otherwise taken component-wise, with denies unioned so that no hop and no intent can lift a deny.

Resource identifiers MUST be canonical. File-system paths MUST be absolute and normalized, with the home directory expanded and ".." collapsed. URLs MUST carry their resolved host class. SaaS objects MUST be identified as provider:type/id. A verifier MUST NOT rely on user-relative forms.

An effect is x = (a, r, d, e, t, v), where v is an OPTIONAL quantity. x ⊨ C if and only if some grant of C permits both a and r, a matches no pattern of A⁻, r matches no pattern of R⁻, e ≤ E, every released (data class, recipient class) pair is in D, and t ∈ V.
A claim set that carries a member this document does not define, and that is not an extension member, makes the result unresolved (I7): ignoring a member that narrows authority could widen it.

section.name: Limits
section.t: A limit caps a quantity of one unit, such as iso4217:EUR, an asset, or count:records, with an OPTIONAL maximum per effect, per call (the total of one invocation's effects), and per period (a total within fixed windows of a stated length, starting at the node's validity start). An effect's quantity is an exact decimal string and a unit. Amounts are compared exactly, never as floating point.

list.t: For every node on the chain that carries limits, every limit that applies to an effect is checked before the result is decided. A violation takes precedence over an unresolved check, so the result does not depend on the order in which limits are listed.

A period total is the verifier's running total for the window, including state carried from earlier packets (). A period total reported by an observer counts only if the limit names that observer as the one that counts all of the node's spending in the unit, and only if the observer's figure states the start of the window it covers and that start equals the limit's window start. An observer's figure for a different window would otherwise understate the limit's total, or blame an honest observer.

Without such a figure and without earlier state for the window, the period total is unknown, and the result is unresolved (I7). A packet's assembler can leave out earlier effects, so a period total is never assumed to start at zero.
An approval that passed I8 authorizes its effect to exceed a limit. The approved amount still counts toward the period total.

section.name: Signer Roles
section.t: A valid signature shows only that a key signed a record. Each key in the verifier's key set carries roles, and a record counts as signed only when its key holds a role permitted for the record's kind:
Without roles, a compromised host key could mint its own mandate or approve its own action.

Ed25519 signatures are accepted under one exact rule in every verifier. A verifier MUST reject a signature whose scalar S is not less than the group order, and a public key or commitment R whose encoding is non-canonical or is a point of small order. Libraries otherwise differ on these edge cases (one accepts a signature by the identity key over every message), and two verifiers would then disagree on the same record.

section.name: Call Statements
section.t: An effect record says what was executed. It cannot say that nothing was. A call statement is the observer's signed account of one call: its disposition (completed, not executed, or failed after the effects it counts), the number of effect records it issued for the call, and OPTIONALLY the digest of the exact signed invocation and of the arguments it received.

list.t: A statement that does not verify, has an unknown disposition, or says "not executed" while counting effects, makes the result unresolved (I7).

A statement or effect record bound to a different invocation (by invocation digest) is not evidence for this one: unresolved (I7). A genuine record for one call therefore cannot be presented for another call that reuses its identifier.
If the arguments the observer received differ from those the host signed, the call was changed in transit: violated (I2), or unresolved (I7) when nothing was executed.
An effect record for a call the observer says was not executed is equivocation: violated (I11).

With no effect records and a verified "not executed" statement, the call provably had no effect, and the result is preserved. For a call at or above write_shared, the statement must come from a party other than the actor; otherwise unresolved (I10).

section.t: Without a call statement, an invocation with no effect record is unresolved (I7): the effect may have happened. A refusal by a gateway is therefore recorded as a "not executed" statement signed by the gateway, never as an absence of records.

section.name: Evaluation Procedure
section.t: For each invocation, in recorded order, a verifier MUST apply the following checks in order and return the first outcome that applies, except where a group is marked as checked in full. "Verified" means signed by a key holding a permitted role ().

see State Across Packets) For every effect record of the invocation: I7 unresolved record not verified, names no observer, or is bound to a different invocation I10 unresolved e >= write_shared and the actor is absent, the effect is self-observed, or assurance L0 I6 violated revoked at or before the effect's own time (unresolved inside a propagation window, or when status is not fresh as of that time) I2 violated executed != declared (and != the mediated effect) I9 violated executed resource is a guardrail I2 violated x does not satisfy the meet of the chain and intent (I5 when the failure is a release) I5 violated data classes carried in through lineage reach a recipient class the claims do not permit I7 violated more effect records than the call statement counts I7 unresolved fewer effect records than it counts I7 unresolved approval missing or not verified I8 violated approval unbound, outside its window, consumed, reused, or covering an effect fewer times than it was executed Limits (see Limits), every applicable limit checked in full: I2 violated over a per-effect, per-call or per-period limit without a bound approval I7 violated the counting observer's total for the window is below the effects recorded I7 unresolved period total unknown, or held calls could take it over the limit I7 violated recorded budget spend != recomputed cost I2 violated risk budget exceeded without a bound approval - preserved otherwise

section.t: After all invocations:

figure.artwork: ID Outcome Condition I11 violated pre-execution deny/hold decision, and an effect exists (enforcement contradicted) - preserved pre-execution deny/hold decision, no effect, enforcement fail-closed or applied = confirmed I11 violated effect with no invocation

section.t: The packet verdict is the first violated result if there is one, else the first unresolved result, else preserved.

Lineage: an effect may record the data classes it read (accessed) and the recipient class of what it sent; an invocation may name the earlier invocations its input came from (derived_from). The data classes an invocation carries are those its own effects read plus those carried by the invocations it derives from, transitively. This detects sensitive data leaving in a later step even when that step declares no release.

Decisions carry a phase: pre_execution, post_execution, or simulation. Only pre-execution decisions can confirm or contradict a block. A post-execution decision is detection and MUST NOT be presented as having prevented the action.

When B is present, the cost of x is base(e) × m(d) × rev(x). The base table is read 0, write_local 1, write_shared 3, external_send 5, destructive 10, financial 20. m(d) is the largest data-class multiplier among the released classes (1, 2, or 5). rev(x) is 1 if the effect is a read, or reversible and not an external send, and 3 otherwise. The cost is charged to every node in the chain. The tables are registries ().

section.name: Approvals
section.t: An approval binds the digest of the exact effect it approves: SHA-256 over the JCS form of the effect without its time and without any observer's running totals, so that it can be issued before execution. An operation approval instead lists the digests of the effects of one call, for example an operation that writes two files. Every executed effect of that call must be listed, and no effect may run more often than it is listed. Either form is single use: a retry that cites it again is violated (I8).

section.name: Results: Blame and Missing Evidence
section.t: Each result carries two further members, derived only from the signed evidence. A verifier MUST NOT infer blame the evidence does not show.

list.t: blame (violated results only) names the party whose own signed record is the first to depart from authority: agent (it asked for or acted on something not allowed), delegator (a delegation widened its parent), host (the host or enforcement point failed at its own role), transport (the arguments received differ from those signed), or server (the executing party's records contradict the authorized call or each other).

gaps (unresolved results only) lists the evidence that would let the evaluation continue, each as a need and the identifier of the record concerned, for example a missing effect record, a fresh revocation status, an independent observer, or the outcome of a held call.

section.name: State Across Packets
section.t: A verifier evaluating a stream of packets MAY carry state from one packet to the next: approval use, risk-budget spending, and per-window period totals. Within one stream, state MUST be passed in time order.

A verified invocation that ends a packet with no effect record and no "not executed" statement may still have executed. Its outcome is unknown, and the verifier records a hold in its state against every period limit on its chain that applies to it: the amount the invocation declared as the most it can move, or an unknown amount if it declared none. In later packets, every hold whose invocation is not in that packet counts toward the same window's total. A total that could exceed the limit with the holds added, or an unknown held amount, makes the result unresolved (I7), never violated, because the held call may not have executed. A later packet that contains the held invocation replaces its hold: its effect records then count as any other, a "not executed" statement releases it, and a hold is never counted twice. Only a verified invocation can be held, so evidence that does not verify cannot place holds.

This follows the requirement, raised in a cross-institution example of delegated payment authority , that a slice with an unknown outcome stays counted until reconciliation shows whether it was booked.
State is the verifier's own bookkeeping, not evidence. A verifier that relies on it SHOULD publish the state it used alongside its verdict records.

section.name: Verdict Records
section.t: A verifier MAY publish what it concluded as a verdict record: the predicate of an in-toto Statement v1 whose subject is the SHA-256 of the exact packet bytes evaluated. The predicate gives the SHA-256 of the JCS form of the key set, the packet verdict, and every result in evaluation order, each with its outcome, invariant, blame and gaps. Free-text reasons are excluded, because they differ between implementations.

Two conforming verifiers given the same packet and key set MUST produce byte-identical JCS forms of the record once the member naming the implementation is removed. A verdict record is therefore re-derivable: a party that trusts neither the agent nor its operator, nor the first auditor, can evaluate the same packet and compare. A signed verdict record is the statement carried in a DSSE envelope , signed with Ed25519.
A verdict record is one verifier's reading of the evidence, not evidence of what the agent did. In a dispute, the packet is the evidence.

section.name: Required Fields
section.t: The evaluation needs the following fields from each AUDIT record. Field names are placeholders until the AUDIT data model is defined.

list.t: Mandate, Intent, and Delegation: id, parent, issuer, claims (C), signature.

Invocation: id, authority reference, interpretation reference (adapter and version), declared effect, actor, influence references, approval reference, time; OPTIONALLY the digest of the arguments sent, and the most the call can move (its reserve).

Effect: id, invocation reference, OPTIONAL invocation digest, executed effect x, observer, assurance level (L0 self-reported to L3 provider-confirmed), signature. A quantity carries an amount, a unit, and OPTIONALLY the observer's own totals, each with the start of the window it covers.
Call statement: id, invocation reference, observer, disposition, effect count, time, OPTIONAL invocation digest and arguments digest, signature.
Approval: id, effect digest or list of effect digests, presence (webauthn, chat_user, host_ui, or none), validity window, consumed flag, signature.
Revocation and revocation status: target, time (or as-of time and revocation time), OPTIONAL propagation window on the revocable node, signature.
Continuity decision: invocation reference, mode, phase, outcome, enforcement context (enforcement point, fail mode, what was returned to the host, whether an effect record confirms it), signature.

section.t: Records are canonicalized with JCS and signed with Ed25519 over a domain-separated signing input. Times are numbers of seconds since the epoch or RFC 3339 strings. A CDDL definition and JSON Schemas are published in .

A packet that is not well-formed I-JSON within the bounds the specification sets (duplicate member names, numbers outside the safe-integer range, lone surrogates, excessive nesting) makes every invocation in it unresolved (I7): such a packet cannot be canonicalized to the same bytes by every verifier. Values whose exact identity matters, such as amounts and identifiers, SHOULD be strings.
A packet MAY declare the version of the rules it was produced for. A verifier MUST treat a packet declaring a version it does not implement as malformed.

section.name: Test Vectors
section.t: publishes three suites of signed packets, each with an expected outcome and invariant: 233 core vectors (62 positive and 171 must-reject), 16 approval-path vectors, and 20 delegation-continuity vectors, 269 in all. The must-reject vectors cover all eleven invariants, signer roles, the Ed25519 acceptance rule, malformed I-JSON, revocation at the time of each effect, call statements and binding, operation approvals, grants, limits checked independently of their order, observer totals for the wrong window, held calls across packets, decision phase, deny lists, data lineage, and state across packets.

Two implementations written separately by the author (Python, and JavaScript run under Node.js and in a browser) agree on all 269, on the outcome, invariant, blame and gaps of every result, and produce byte-identical verdict records. Implementations by other parties are invited. A conformance tool runs any verifier that can be invoked from a command line against all three suites.
A conforming verifier MUST return the expected outcome and invariant for every vector.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: Note to the RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication, per .

list.t: AMEP reference verifiers. Two implementations, both by the author: Python (package amep-protocol 0.3.0a2) and JavaScript (package @stafordtituss/amep 0.3.0-alpha.2, published with build provenance), the latter also run as an offline browser page using WebCrypto. Both evaluate the procedure in , agree on all 269 published vectors, and produce byte-identical verdict records. License: Apache 2.0. Location: https://github.com/stafordtituss/amep. Maturity: prototype.

AMEP conformance tool and import profiles. It runs a verifier against the suites, and re-expresses records of other formats as evidence after checking them by their own rules: AER-1 receipts, OpenID action receipts, and Provared permission books. It also compares AMEP's results with the published test vectors of the Delegation Receipt Protocol and of EMILIA Protocol authorization receipts. Location: as above.
AMEP MCP server. Exposes the verifier and the suites to MCP clients; listed in the MCP Registry. Location: as above.
Natsar control plane (agent-authority enforcement for coding-agent hosts and MCP). It emits decision records before tool execution from host hooks. Maturity: pre-release.

section.t: Use and review by other parties, each in a public record:

list.t: AER-1 (Brennan Zambo). An import run over twelve live receipts from a production MCP server, with the implementer's own tool map. It found that a gateway refusal was imported as an executed effect; the importer was corrected. A later run over two re-issued records was blind, with the expected results committed before either side ran it, and both sides' results matched.

Verifiable Agent Trust Envelope (Takao Sato). The maintainer verified the signatures of five published verdict records for a lost-response and recovery case, matched each to its packet by digest, and reviewed a reference example of the case.

Payments review (Carlos Vendrell Felici, Zealynx Security). Two rounds of review of the quantity limits, with signed test packets run through both verifiers. They led to the per-call and per-effect limits, per-observer counting of effects, the counting observer, integer amounts for on-chain assets, independent totals per limit, order-independent evaluation of limits, and observer totals that name their window.
AUDIT mailing list review (Cliff Singletary). Led to evaluating revocation and status freshness at the time of each effect, not only at the invocation.

section.t: Implementation experience motivated several parts of this document: canonical resource identifiers (absolute-path forms bypassed relative-prefix rules); recording the enforcement context and phase (hosts differ in whether they support "ask" and whether hook failures block); treating an effect that contradicts a deny as evidence of bypass; and the call statement, without which a refusal and a lost response are indistinguishable from each other.

list.t: Adversarial models: the guarantees MUST hold even if every model in the chain is adversarial. Semantic analysis MAY raise a decision level, but MUST NOT mint authority or lower a decision.
Self-reporting: records produced by the actor alone are insufficient for high-impact effects, including a statement that nothing was executed (I10).
Key compromise: signer roles () limit what one stolen key can forge.

Evidence omission: a missing record, status or signature yields unresolved. A call with no outcome is held across packets (), so leaving its outcome out of later packets cannot make a later total look clean. Omission of whole invocations is detected only against an independent effect log (I11).
Record substitution: binding effect records and call statements to the digest of the exact invocation prevents a genuine record for one call from being presented for another.
Canonicalization: non-canonical resource forms and non-canonical JSON enable bypasses and disagreement between verifiers. Canonicalization is therefore normative.
Approval replay and time-of-check/time-of-use: approvals bind the exact effect or effects and are single use (I8). Liveness is checked at the time of each effect, not only at the invocation (I6).

Fail-open enforcement: an enforcement point that errors MUST return a deny decision, not a transport error. A verifier SHOULD treat an effect that contradicts a pre-execution deny as evidence of bypass.
Guardrail tampering: agent writes to hook configuration, keys, instruction files, or the audit store are violations (I9).
Verdict records: a verdict record is a claim by its signer. Relying parties SHOULD re-derive it from the packet, which the determinism in allows.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Effect records can contain personal data. Verifiers need only canonical actions, resource identifiers, data-class labels, quantities, and digests. Payloads SHOULD be detached and hashed, following the AUDIT selective-disclosure work. A verdict record names packets by digest and carries no payload.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document proposes registries for effect classes, data classes, recipient classes, signer roles, call statement dispositions, blame values, gap names, and the risk-cost tables, with the registration policy Specification Required. The registries are to be defined in a later revision.

front.title: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)

abstract.t: Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing need the data to be expressed in an invariant format so that the operations are reliably repeatable. One way to address this is to create a canonical representation of the data. Canonicalization also permits data to be exchanged in its original form on the "wire" while cryptographic operations performed on the canonicalized counterpart of the data in the producer and consumer endpoints generate consistent results.

This document describes the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS). This specification defines how to create a canonical representation of JSON data by building on the strict serialization methods for JSON primitives defined by ECMAScript, constraining JSON data to the Internet JSON (I-JSON) subset, and by using deterministic property sorting.

front.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)

abstract.t: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: The I-JSON Message Format

abstract.t: I-JSON (short for "Internet JSON") is a restricted profile of JSON designed to maximize interoperability and increase confidence that software can process it successfully with predictable results.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL): A Notational Convention to Express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and JSON Data Structures

abstract.t: This document proposes a notational convention to express Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) data structures (RFC 7049). Its main goal is to provide an easy and unambiguous way to express structures for protocol messages and data formats that use CBOR or JSON.

front.title: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange

abstract.t: This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP)

abstract.t: The Grant Negotiation and Authorization Protocol (GNAP) defines a mechanism for delegating authorization to a piece of software and conveying the results and artifacts of that delegation to the software. This delegation can include access to a set of APIs as well as subject information passed directly to the software.

front.title: An Architecture for Auditing Agent Delegation and Interactions

abstract.t: This document describes an architecture for auditing of agent-driven interactions on the Internet. Autonomous and semi-autonomous software agents, including those based on artificial intelligence, increasingly act on behalf of users, organizations, and services. Existing auditing mechanisms often capture isolated system events but do not consistently represent delegation relationships, user intent, or evolving authorization. In agent-driven systems, auditability requires linking intent, delegation, authorization, and execution. The proposed architecture enables this through distributed audit record generation, propagation of audit context, optional attestation, and additional logging for transparency.

front.title: Verifiable Agent Conversation Records

abstract.t: Autonomous agents based on large language models increasingly perform consequential tasks on behalf of humans and other agents. Demonstrating that recorded agent behavior truthfully represents actual behavior is essential for accountability, compliance, and human oversight. This document defines a data format for verifiable agent conversation records using CDDL, with representations in both JSON and CBOR. The format captures session metadata, message exchanges, tool invocations, reasoning traces, and system events in a structured, extensible CDDL definition for verifiable agent conversation records. COSE is used as the signing method to allow for native interoperability in SCITT Transparency Services and the CDDL definition allows for seemless integration in Evidence as specified in RFC 9334. The specification supports cross-vendor interoperability by defining a common representation that accommodates translation from multiple existing agent implementations with distinct data structure layouts that are typically represented in JSON.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While verifiable data structures have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility, interoperability between different transparency services, and compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: Agent Delegation Receipts

abstract.t: This document defines the Agent Delegation Receipt: a signed record of what a human principal authorized an AI agent to do, for how long, and under what instructions. The receipt carries a scope, hard boundaries, a validity window, and a hash of the operator's stated instructions, all signed by the authorizing key. Version -11 replaces the draft's earlier custom signature format with two standard profiles: a JWS profile (RFC 7515) over JCS-canonicalized JSON (RFC 8785) as the primary wire format, and a COSE_Sign1 profile (RFC 9052) for constrained environments. It also specifies scope attenuation rules for multi-agent delegation chains, a revocation registry model with cascade semantics, and the limitations of what receipts can and cannot prove. Version -12 resolves the unknown- fields question raised on the IETF oauth mailing list: authorization fields are closed (verifiers reject unknown top-level body fields rather than silently ignoring them), the "metadata" object is the defined extension point, and one-time-use receipts fail closed without a durable consumption store. Version -13 incorporates independent-implementation feedback: it pins the orchestratorSignature verification key to the sub-receipt signer's key, states the receipt-issuance computation order explicitly, and guides issuers on default boundaries versus explicit allowances. Version -14 adds a pointer to content profiles for verification of what the agent produced, following implementer feedback. Version -15 adopts the grant/execution vocabulary of [CHEN-AGENT-USE-CASES]: the receipt as Execution Layer Evidence for a Grant Layer Authority. It adds delegatee holder binding for sub-receipts -- a parent names the delegatee's public key, closing a bearer-copy issuance gap found in review -- deprecates orchestratorSignature as redundant, sketches an OAuth authorization_details binding so a token can reference its receipt, and states normative custody requirements for the authorizing key. The delegateeKey field is a wire-format addition; -14-era verifiers will reject receipts carrying it, which is the intended fail-closed version behavior.
